questions.q: Which four AdventureWorks2012 tables does this report's plain-English plan identify as needed?
questions.explain: Each table answers one part of the question: SalesOrderDetail for amounts, SalesOrderHeader for date and territory ID, Product for product line, SalesTerritory for a readable region name.

questions.q: What column connects Sales.SalesOrderDetail to Sales.SalesOrderHeader?
questions.explain: SalesOrderDetail and SalesOrderHeader both carry SalesOrderID, which is the join key linking a line item back to its order.

questions.q: Why does the plan start from Sales.SalesOrderDetail rather than Sales.SalesOrderHeader?
options: SalesOrderHeader does not contain a TerritoryID column
The dollar amount being totaled (LineTotal) lives on the detail table, and starting there avoids double-counting an order's total once per line item
T-SQL requires queries to start from the table with the most rows
questions.explain: Starting from the table that holds the number you're aggregating, and joining outward, prevents the common mistake of double-counting header-level totals.

questions.q: In this report's grouping plan, what does a single output row represent?
options: One unique combination of sales territory and product line
questions.explain: The grain of the report is one row per territory-and-product-line pairing, which is why the GROUP BY needs both columns together.

questions.q: What is the purpose of writing a plain-English join plan before opening SSMS?
options: To avoid ever having to write a WHERE clause
To confirm you can name every table and every join key before translating the plan into real SQL syntax
To replace the need for a GROUP BY clause entirely
Because T-SQL cannot join more than two tables at once
questions.explain: If you can't state the join key in plain English, the lesson argues you're not ready to write the JOIN yet — the sketch catches gaps before they become SQL errors.
